Core Thesis

Experiencing attraction to or interest in someone else while in a committed relationship does not invalidate your love for your partner; this is a normal human experience that differs from possessive or "toxic monogamy" beliefs that equate real love with complete emotional exclusivity.

Key Points

  • Interest in others during a committed relationship is a normal human experience, not a sign of insufficient love or relationship failure.

  • Polyamorous and non-monogamous people demonstrate that love and interest in multiple people can coexist; their experience challenges the false equation between monogamy and genuine love.
  • External interest can provide useful self-reflection: examining unmet needs, childhood attachment wounds, or relationship gaps rather than automatically acting on the attraction.
  • Sometimes attraction to others is simply a fleeting, non-loaded feeling that fades naturally without requiring action or acknowledgment—this is also fine and normal.

    • Takeaways

  • If you experience attraction to someone else in your relationship, pause before assuming it signals a problem; use it as information to understand your own needs rather than as a threat to your partnership.
  • Be cautious of relationship advice that prescribes one "correct" emotional experience; what works for one person's attachment style may not apply universally and can create unnecessary shame or doubt.

item.author: Self Experimenting
item.description:
Category: Psychology & Mental Health  |  Score: 8/10  |  Creator: Self Experimenting

▶️ Watch on YouTube

Category

Psychology & Mental Health

Core Thesis

Time blindness in ADHD extends beyond task timing to affect how individuals perceive their identity and progress over time, leading to disconnection from self, avoidance cycles, and self-sabotage. Understanding this mechanism is key to breaking these patterns.

Key Points

  • Time blindness prevents individuals from recognizing how time progresses generally, causing them to over-identify with their present moment state rather than seeing themselves across different time periods or "seasons"
  • The condition creates an oscillating pattern: either an urgent "fix it now" impulse (fearing they won't remember later) or avoidance paralysis (because the future feels unreal and unreachable)
  • Disconnection from past accomplishments and confident versions of oneself makes it difficult to maintain goal motivation, as positive memories become inaccessible when needed
  • Self-sabotage often results from underestimating task duration combined with avoidance cycles—people abandon goals mid-pursuit without understanding why they started them
  • Visual external tools (written identity statements, progress photos, habit trackers) compensate by moving information out of the brain where memory fails

    • Takeaways

  • If you have ADHD time blindness, document your identity, values, and past wins visually (wall posters, progress photos) and review them daily to create an external reference point your brain can trust
  • Notice whether you're in a "urgency cycle" or "avoidance cycle" when pursuing goals—recognizing the pattern helps you adjust your approach rather than interpreting it as personal failure
  • Consider using visual trackers and progress documentation not as perfectionism tools, but as compensatory systems that bridge the gap between your lived experience and your brain's ability to retain it

Lifestyle inflation—spending more as income increases—is a major barrier to wealth building because it locks people into higher fixed costs, making it difficult to save or invest despite earning more money.

  • Many people delay financial progress (debt payoff, investing) by telling themselves they'll act "once they earn more," but the cycle repeats because raises get absorbed into spending rather than savings.

    • Takeaways

  • Be intentional about large purchases (cars, homes, upgrades) and question whether they create unsustainable monthly obligations that trap your future income.
